extracted.intended_audience: Employers, employees, labor and management representatives, state agencies, standards organizations, and other interested persons involved in or affected by OSHA rulemaking and variance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Official guidance on how OSHA initiates, develops, proposes, adopts, and litigates standards, and on procedures and requirements for variances, interim orders, and emergency temporary standards. Covers who may petition, advisory committees, public notice and comment, hearings, and requirements for temporary/permanent/experimental variances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may petition OSHA for standards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA can begin standards-setting procedures on its own initiative, or in response to petitions from other parties, including the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS); the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH); state and local governments; any nationally-recognized standards-producing organization; employer or labor representatives; or any other interested person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists authorized petitioning entities; implies that any 'interested person' may petition OSHA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory committees composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: All Advisory committees, standing or ad hoc, must have members representing management, labor, and state agencies, as well as one or more designees of the Secretary of HHS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two standing advisory committees are named (NACOSH and Advisory Committee on Construction Safety and Health); ad hoc committees may be appointed to examine special areas of concern and may be called upon to develop recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIOSH recommendations and investigatory authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH conducts research on various safety and health problems, provides technical assistance to OSHA and recommends standards for OSHA's adoption. While conducting its research, NIOSH may make workplace investigations, gather testimony from employers and employees and require that employers measure and report employee exposure to potentially hazardous materials. NIOSH also may require employers to provide medical examinations and tests to determine the incidence of occupational illness among employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such examinations and tests are required by NIOSH for research purposes, they may be paid for by NIOSH rather than the employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of rulemaking intentions (Advance Notice / NPRM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once OSHA has developed plans to propose, amend or revoke a standard, it publishes these intentions in the Federal Register as a 'Notice of Proposed Rulemaking,' or often as an earlier 'Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.' An 'Advance Notice' is used, when necessary, to solicit information that can be used in drafting a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking will include the terms of the new rule and provide a specific time (at least 30 days from the date of publication, usually 60 days or more) for the public to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with OMB and small business (SBREFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to publication of proposed and final major rules OSHA consults with OMB under procedures established by Executive Order. OSHA consults with small business on proposed rules which significantly affect them through a panel with participation by the Small Business Administration and OMB, as required by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement and Fairness Act (SBREFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates pre-publication interagency and small-business consultation requirements for major rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment period and ability to request hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Interested parties who submit written arguments and pertinent evidence may request a public hearing on the proposal when none has been announced in the notice. When such a hearing is requested, OSHA will schedule one, and will publish, in advance, the time and place for it in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comment periods are specified in the NPRM (at least 30 days, usually 60 or more); request for hearing triggers OSHA to schedule and publish hearing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of final standard and explanatory materials
rubrics_metrics.description: After the close of the comment period and public hearing, if one is held, OSHA must publish in the Federal Register the full, final text of any standard amended or adopted and the date it becomes effective, along with an explanation of the standard and the reasons for implementing it. OSHA may also publish a determination that no standard or amendment needs to be issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rule publication must include effective date and rationale; OSHA may also explicitly determine not to issue a standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Temporary Standards (ETS) substantive criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA must determine that workers are in grave danger due to exposure to toxic substances or agents determined to be toxic or physically harmful or to new hazards and that an emergency standard is needed to protect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ETS take effect immediately and are in effect until superseded by a permanent standard; the ETS also serves as a proposed permanent standard and is subject to the usual adoption procedure except that a final ruling should be made within six months. The validity of an ETS may be challenged in an appropriate U.S. Court of Appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealing a standard: judicial review deadline and effect on enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who may be adversely affected by a final or emergency standard may file a petition (no later than the 59th day after the rule's promulgation) for judicial review of the standard with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the circuit in which the objector lives or has his or her principal place of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an appeals petition will not delay the enforcement of a standard, unless the Court of Appeals specifically orders it.

rubrics_metrics.name: General grounds for seeking a variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may ask OSHA for a variance from a standard or regulation if they cannot fully comply by the effective date, due to shortages of materials, equipment or professional or technical personnel (i.e., temporary variances), or can prove their facilities or methods of operation provide employee protection 'at least as effective' as that required by OSHA (permanent variances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers located in states with their own occupational safety and health programs should apply to the state for a variance. Employers operating in both federal and state-plan states may apply directly to federal OSHA for a single variance applicable to all establishments; OSHA will work with state plan states to determine if a variance can satisfy both state and federal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary variance: eligibility and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary variance may be granted to an employer who cannot comply with a standard or regulation by its effective date due to unavailability of professional or technical personnel, materials or equipment, or because the necessary construction or alteration of facilities cannot be completed in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary variances allow employers to operate while completing compliance steps; application may be made for period needed to achieve compliance or for one year, whichever is shorter, and is renewable twice for six months each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary variance: application content and employer obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a temporary variance must identify the standard or portion of a standard from which the variance is requested and the reasons why the employer cannot comply with the standard. The employer must document those measures already taken and to be taken (including dates) to comply with the standard and establish that all available steps to safeguard employees against the hazards covered by the standard are being taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The employer must certify that workers have been informed of the variance application, that a copy has been given to the employees' authorized representative, and that a summary of the application has been posted wherever notices are normally posted. Employees also must be informed that they have the right to request a hearing on the application. A temporary variance will not be granted to an employer who simply cannot afford to pay for the necessary alterations, equipment, or personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent variance: evidentiary standard and OSHA procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A permanent variance (alternative to a particular requirement or standard) may be granted to employers who prove their conditions, practices, means, methods, operations, or processes provide a safe and healthful workplace as effectively as would compliance with the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA weighs the employer's evidence and arranges a variance inspection and hearing where appropriate. If OSHA finds the request valid, it prescribes a permanent variance detailing the employer's specific exceptions and responsibilities under the ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent variance: employee notification and post-issuance modification
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying for a permanent variance, the employer must inform employees of the application and of their right to request a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anytime after six months from the issuance of a permanent variance, the employer or employees may petition OSHA to modify or revoke it. OSHA also may do this of its own accord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim order: purpose and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: So that employers may continue to operate under existing conditions until a variance decision is made, they may apply to OSHA for an interim order. Application for an interim order may be made either at the same time as, or after, application for a variance. Reasons why the order should be granted may be included in the interim order application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If OSHA denies the request, the employer is notified of the reason for denial. If the interim order is granted, the employer and other concerned parties are informed of the order, and the terms of the order are published in the Federal Register. The employer must inform employees of the order by giving a copy to the authorized employee representative and by posting a copy wherever notices are normally posted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental variance: eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer is participating in an experiment to demonstrate or validate new job safety and health techniques, and that experiment has been approved by either the Secretary of Labor or the Secretary of HHS, a variance may be granted to permit the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental variances enable approved trials of novel safety/health techniques under an approved protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variances for national defense and other special circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to temporary, permanent, and experimental variances, the Secretary of Labor also may find certain variances justified when the national defense is impaired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the nearest OSHA office for further information and assistance in applying for a variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-retroactivity of variances and relationship to citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Variances are not retroactive. An employer who has been cited for a standards violation may not seek relief from the citation by applying for a variance. The fact that a citation is outstanding, however, does not prevent an employer from filing a variance application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that variances cannot be used to overturn prior citations but do not bar filing an application while a citation is outstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to petition for modification or revocation of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers and employees should be aware that, just as they may petition OSHA for the development of standards, they also may petition OSHA for modification or revocation of standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA continually reviews its standards to keep pace with developing and changing industrial technology; public petitions are a mechanism for that review.
